figures.sourceHeading: Preparation of a soluble salt from an insoluble base and acid

specPoints.text: describe an experiment to prepare a pure,dry sample of a soluble salt,starting from an insoluble reactant
practical:prepare a sample of pure,dry hydrated copper(II)sulfate crystals starting from copper(II)oxide

primer.text: You already know from Acids, Alkalis & Titrations that acids react with bases to form salts and water. This practical puts that reaction to work in the laboratory: an insoluble base, copper(II) oxide, is stirred into warm acid until the acid is used up, and the salt it forms is recovered as blue crystals. Every step you will follow exists to keep that product pure and dry.

lessons.title: Method
lessons.opening: This practical makes a familiar blue salt from two simple starting materials: an acid and an insoluble black base. The first stage covers the reaction itself, from warming the acid to adding copper(II) oxide until it is in excess. Filtering then removes the leftover solid, leaving a clean blue solution behind.
keyPoints: The aim is a pure, dry batch of hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals, made from copper(II) oxide.
Warming the dilute sulfuric acid gently speeds up the reaction with the base.
Copper(II) oxide is added slowly to the hot acid and stirred until it is in excess.
Being in excess means the base stops dissolving and a suspension forms in the acid.
Filtering removes the excess solid base, leaving the salt solution in the evaporating basin.

low.restatement: Warm the dilute acid, stir in copper(II) oxide until some solid will no longer dissolve, then filter the mixture.
low.analogy: It is like making hot chocolate: keep stirring in powder until it piles up undissolved at the bottom, then strain the lumps out.
low.examPointer: Learn the apparatus names as well as the steps; the exam hint singles out apparatus names as a common gap.

medium.restatement: The acid reacts with the insoluble base to form the soluble salt in solution; adding base beyond what reacts guarantees every bit of acid is used up, and filtration then removes the unreacted solid.
medium.analogy: Think of inviting just enough guests to finish the food: you keep adding until some are left standing, which proves the food is all gone.
medium.examPointer: Be ready to explain why the base is added in excess: leftover acid would become dangerously concentrated during evaporation.

check.stem: Why is copper(II) oxide added until it is in excess?

options.text: To ensure all of the acid reacts, since leftover acid would become dangerously concentrated later
options.explanation: The practical tip is explicit: excess base uses up all the acid before evaporation.

options.text: To make the reaction go faster
options.explanation: The amount added does not change the rate; warming the acid does that.

options.text: To dissolve the salt more quickly
options.explanation: The base does not dissolve the salt; it reacts with the acid to form it.

options.text: To make the crystals turn blue
options.explanation: The colour comes from hydrated copper(II) sulfate itself, not from the amount of base.

check.stem: How do you know when the base is in excess?

options.text: Some solid stops dissolving and a suspension remains however much you stir
options.explanation: The note defines the endpoint as the base stopping dissolving with a suspension left in the acid.

options.text: The solution turns from blue to colourless
options.explanation: The solution turns blue as the salt forms; colour is not the endpoint signal.

options.text: The mixture stops fizzing
options.explanation: This reaction is not gas-evolving; fizzing belongs to the carbonate and acid test.

options.text: The acid stops bubbling when heated
options.explanation: Warming causes no bubbling here; the endpoint is the undissolved solid.

check.stem: What is the purpose of the filtration step?

options.text: To remove the excess, unreacted copper(II) oxide from the salt solution
options.explanation: The solid caught on the paper is the leftover base; the filtrate is the salt solution.

options.text: To remove unreacted acid from the solution
options.explanation: The acid was already consumed by the excess base before filtering.

options.text: To separate the blue salt from the water
options.explanation: The salt stays dissolved in the filtrate; crystallisation comes later.

options.text: To purify the crystals before drying
options.explanation: No crystals exist yet; filtration happens well before evaporation.

check.stem: Why is the acid warmed before the base is added?

options.text: Gentle warming speeds up the reaction between the acid and the base
options.explanation: Warmer particles react faster, so the base dissolves and reacts sooner.

options.text: To evaporate the acid before mixing
options.explanation: Evaporating the acid would be dangerous and would defeat the reaction.

options.text: To melt the copper(II) oxide
options.explanation: Copper(II) oxide stays solid; the warming serves the reaction rate of the acid.

options.text: To make the filtrate easier to filter
options.explanation: Filtration ease is not the reason; the warming is about reaction speed.

check.stem: Which piece of apparatus collects the salt solution after filtration?

options.text: The evaporating basin
options.explanation: The method filters the mixture into an evaporating basin ready for concentration.

options.text: The conical flask
options.explanation: The flask appears in the materials list, but the filtrate is collected in the evaporating basin.

options.text: The measuring cylinder
options.explanation: It measures the 50 cm3 of acid at the start; it never collects the filtrate.

options.text: The filter funnel
options.explanation: The funnel directs the filtrate; the basin beneath it receives the liquid.

lessons.title: Results
lessons.opening: The second stage turns the blue solution into the crystals the exam asks for. Evaporation concentrates the solution until it is saturated, a cold glass rod confirms the point is reached, and crystallisation is then left to happen on its own. The final crystals should be bright blue and regularly shaped.
keyPoints: The solution is heated gently to evaporate water and make it saturated.
Dipping a cold glass rod into the solution checks saturation, as crystals form on the end.
The filtrate is left in a warm place to dry and crystallise.
Excess solution is decanted away, and the crystals are allowed to dry.
Good crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate are bright blue and regularly shaped.

low.restatement: Heat the filtered solution gently to saturate it, test with a cold glass rod, then leave it to crystallise and dry.
low.analogy: It is like reducing a soup until a spoonful coats the spoon: the cold rod is your taste test, and crystals forming mean the liquid can hold no more.
low.examPointer: Describe the crystals as bright blue and regularly shaped when asked for the expected results, and know the apparatus used at every stage.

medium.restatement: Gentle heating drives off water until the solution is saturated, which the cold-rod test confirms; slow crystallisation in a warm place follows, then decanting and drying leave the pure hydrated crystals.
medium.analogy: Picture the solution as a crowded train: as water evaporates, the salt can no longer all fit in solution, so it steps out in an orderly line as crystals.
medium.examPointer: Water-bath or electric heating is specified for evaporation; the direct Bunsen flame was only for the initial warming, a distinction worth knowing.

check.stem: How is the solution heated during the evaporation stage?

options.text: Gently, in a water bath or with an electric heater, until the solution is saturated
options.explanation: The method specifies gentle evaporation; the Bunsen was only for the initial warming of the acid.

options.text: Fiercely with a Bunsen burner until it boils dry
options.explanation: Boiling dry would spatter the salt and is never the method.

options.text: It is not heated; the solution is simply left in sunlight
options.explanation: The method requires controlled heating to reach saturation.

options.text: The evaporating basin is heated directly over the Bunsen flame
options.explanation: The method calls for a water bath or electric heater at this stage.

check.stem: What does the cold glass rod test show?

options.text: That the solution is saturated: crystals forming on the rod show no more salt can dissolve
options.explanation: A cold surface triggers crystallisation only when the solution is saturated.

options.text: That the solution is still too dilute to use
options.explanation: Crystals on the rod mean saturation has been reached, not failure.

options.text: That the solution has become dangerously concentrated
options.explanation: Saturation is the desired state before crystallisation, not a hazard signal.

options.text: That the rod has been contaminated with base
options.explanation: The test reports the state of the solution, not the cleanliness of the rod.

check.stem: Why must the leftover acid have been removed before this stage?

options.text: Because during evaporation and crystallisation the acid would become dangerously concentrated
options.explanation: The practical tip places the danger exactly in this stage, which is why the base was added in excess.

options.text: Because acid would make the crystals green instead of blue
options.explanation: The risk named is concentration and danger, not a colour change.

options.text: Because acid would stop the water evaporating
options.explanation: Evaporation is unaffected; the danger is the concentrated acid itself.

options.text: Because the filter paper would dissolve in acid
options.explanation: Filtration is already complete; the concern is the evaporation stage.

check.stem: What should the finished crystals look like?

options.text: Bright blue and regularly shaped
options.explanation: That is the note's stated appearance for hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals.

options.text: White and powdery
options.explanation: White is the anhydrous form; this preparation yields the hydrated blue crystals.

options.text: Green and irregular
options.explanation: Green is not the expected colour; the hydrated crystals are bright blue.

options.text: Colourless and cube-shaped
options.explanation: The crystals are distinctly blue; colourless would suggest no copper compound at all.

check.stem: After crystallisation, how are the crystals finally obtained dry?

options.text: The excess solution is decanted off and the crystals are left to dry
options.explanation: The method's last steps are decanting the excess solution and letting the crystals dry.

options.text: They are heated strongly with a Bunsen burner until bone dry
options.explanation: Strong heating would drive off the water of crystallisation and spoil the hydrated crystals.

options.text: They are rinsed thoroughly with water
options.explanation: Rinsing would dissolve the crystals you just made.

options.text: They are scraped from the filter paper
options.explanation: Filtration belonged to the earlier stage; the crystals grow in the basin.

glossary.definition: A crystal containing water molecules within its structure; the blue form of copper(II) sulfate is hydrated.
A substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water; copper(II) oxide is the base here.
Added beyond the amount that reacts; some solid remains undissolved, proving the acid has been used up.
A mixture in which fine solid particles are held in a liquid without dissolving.
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid by filter paper; the liquid passing through is the filtrate.
Holding as much dissolved salt as possible at that temperature, so crystals can form.
The change of a liquid into a gas at the surface; here it concentrates the salt solution.
The formation of solid crystals from a saturated solution as it cools or dries.

workedExample.prompt: Describe how to prepare pure, dry hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide, including how you would know the base is in excess and the solution is saturated.
steps: Warm dilute sulfuric acid gently in a beaker, then add black copper(II) oxide slowly with stirring until it stops dissolving and a suspension forms — that shows the base is in excess and all the acid has reacted.
Filter the mixture into an evaporating basin to remove the excess solid base.
Heat the blue filtrate gently in a water bath to evaporate water; dip a cold glass rod into the solution — small crystals forming on the end shows the solution is saturated.
Leave the filtrate in a warm place to crystallise, decant the excess solution and allow the bright blue, regularly shaped crystals to dry.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Warm acid, add excess CuO, filter, evaporate to saturation (cold-rod test), crystallise, decant and dry.
